brief.head: Ten thousand universes
brief.text: Economics has out­grown its “physics il­lu­sion”, Ajay Shah said. With about 10,000 im­por­tant datasets, each its own lit­tle uni­verse, it now solves one puz­zle at a time. {#datasets}

brief.head: Diabetes, by country
brief.text: Even medicine can turn local, Shah said: if Indian DNA mat­ters, di­a­betes in India may dif­fer from di­a­betes in China. Physics, by con­trast, is uni­ver­sal. {062-C03}

brief.head: Marx’s epitaph
brief.text: Some re­search seeks only to un­der­stand the world, Shah said; some aims to act in it, in the spirit of Karl Marx’s epi­taph: “the point, how­ever, is to change it.” {062-J14}

brief.head: A bonfire of journals
brief.text: Amit Varma pro­posed a party: get every aca­demic they know com­pletely drunk, gather a bunch of jour­nals, and hold “a bon­fire of the jour­nals”. {062-J05}

brief.head: Who gets the byline
brief.text: Authors in­vent and as­sis­tants im­ple­ment, Ajay Shah said. Assistants are thanked on the front page; only orig­i­nal cre­ative work earns au­thor­ship. {#authors}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah gives a masterclass on research writing
lead.head: Gentle readers, gentle writers

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 62

body: Ajay Shah promised at the out­set that by the end of his mas­ter­class on how to write a paper, “our gen­tle read­ers will be­come gen­tle writ­ers”. {062-J01}

Amit Varma made clear the hour was not only for aca­demics. Think of a paper, he said, as a proxy for any at­tempt at a novel in­sight: how to or­gan­ise knowl­edge, what rigour it needs, how to craft and struc­ture it.
The struc­ture of what you write, Varma ar­gued, shapes the struc­ture of how you think. So this was also meant as a mas­ter­class on how to think.
Shah de­fined the word just as broadly. A paper, for him, is a unit of knowl­edge: a news­pa­per ar­ti­cle, a blog post, a work­ing paper or a jour­nal ar­ti­cle. New in­sight is what counts.
## The ma­chine and its gate­keep­ers

Varma began with Larry White’s pic­ture of an idea pipe­line, from lonely re­searchers to com­men­ta­tors to the pub­lic, and asked whether it still works. In an ear­lier episode, the hosts had ar­gued that much of academia has be­come a cir­cle game.
Shah was frank about jour­nals. They once spread knowl­edge; now they hand out cre­den­tials.
“Journal pub­li­ca­tion is there for the sole pur­pose of cre­den­tials,” he said. “I got a pub in this jour­nal, please give me a job, please give me a grant.” {062-C04}
A good paper, he said, needs a clear ques­tion, a per­sua­sive an­swer and nov­elty. {062-C05}
Which ques­tions count as im­por­tant is an­other mat­ter, and Shah re­jected the gatekeepers’ snob­bery. Varma went fur­ther: peer re­view, he said, makes him want to puke.
## Writing for the reader
Varma brought in the les­son of his writ­ing course. Communication has two vari­ables, you and your reader, and most writ­ers ig­nore the sec­ond.

Shah agreed. Writing a re­search paper, he said, “is a lot more like writ­ing than re­searchers care to admit”. Readers do not want the researcher’s life story, only the ques­tion, the ap­proach and the find­ings.
He of­fered struc­tures to start from: IMRD for sci­ence pa­pers, and an eco­nom­ics recipe that opens with a 1,000-word sum­mary dis­guised as an in­tro­duc­tion.
His rule of thumb for read­er­ship is sober­ing. About 100,000 peo­ple see a paper’s title, 10,000 read the ab­stract, 1,000 start the paper and 100 fin­ish it. {062-C12}

So he writes in­side out: the body first, then the con­clu­sions, the in­tro­duc­tion and the ab­stract, and the title last. His teams first build each paper as a dense in­ter­nal slideshow, re­fined meet­ing by meet­ing until it stops chang­ing.
## After the last full stop
A fin­ished paper still has to be pushed, through blog posts, news­pa­per pieces, videos and talks. Shah prefers small rooms, where ten fo­cused peo­ple can be per­suaded, to big con­fer­ences.
He does not think the world picked his best pa­pers, and he is at peace with that.
None of it comes quickly. A sad fact of the mod­ern world, Shah said, is that “most peo­ple who have fin­ished a PhD are ac­tu­ally quite bad at writ­ing pa­pers”. {062-C16}
His rec­om­men­da­tions were for the craft it­self: the sim­ple Strunk and White, and Varma’s *Art of Clear Writing* course.
Varma had a griev­ance of a dif­fer­ent kind. Authors are often listed al­pha­bet­i­cally, and his sur­name be­gins with V. “There’s no great econ­o­mist called Zimbalist,” he said.

second.label: Global journals
second.head: Open the windows at home
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why global journals publish SEC trivia but ignore SEBI

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on global journals and SEBI

body: For Indian so­cial sci­en­tists, Ajay Shah said, the night­mare from global jour­nals is a fa­mil­iar ver­dict: “this is not an in­ter­est­ing ques­tion.” {062-S02}

Any ob­scure reg­u­la­tion change at the United States SEC, he said, is wor­thy of the top fi­nance jour­nals. The drama of reg­u­la­tory changes by SEBI, “ar­guably the world’s most ac­tivist fi­nan­cial reg­u­la­tor”, is dis­missed: it’s India. So re­searchers con­tort their work to shed light on “the grand ques­tions of the age as seen in Germany”.

Shah would rather they looked at the re­al­ity around them. That, he said, “cre­ates the en­ergy and the emo­tional re­silience to chase those ques­tions”, and to de­liver their jew­els to the world. {#resilience}

quote.text: I think that we should open the win­dows of our house and look out at the re­al­ity

third.head: Best work, least cited

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the papers the world passed over

body: Amit Varma asked how a cre­ator copes when work is ig­nored. His own habit, he said, is to fin­ish an episode with full in­ten­sity, then for­get it and move on.

Ajay Shah pointed to his page on Google Scholar, where some pa­pers were cited and many were not. “When I look at the list, I don’t agree,” he said. “I don’t think that the world chose my good stuff.” {062-S08}
He is at peace with it. The ar­chive ex­ists, and some­body may come to it a hun­dred years from now. {#archive}

His en­thu­si­asm for any paper suf­fers “some ex­po­nen­tial decay”, he said, so he talks only about work that still ex­cites him: right now, his in­no­va­tion-policy paper with R.A. Mashelkar and Susan Thomas. His rule for talks is sim­ple. “Never do a bor­ing talk.” {#dulltalk}

box.title: The writer’s prescription
box.text: Researchers, Ajay Shah said, grossly un­der­es­ti­mate the craft of writ­ing, ab­sorbed as they are in econo­met­rics or com­puter sci­ence. His pre­scrip­tion: make the sim­ple Strunk and White uni­ver­sal knowl­edge, and at­tend Amit Varma’s *Art of Clear Writing* class. {062-R13}

sections.label: The machine
sections.head: Credentials, not circulation
sections.caption: the sociology of research
body: Amit Varma opened with a pas­sage from Larry White’s *The Clash of Economic Ideas*, which he called a fan­tas­tic book. Ideas, it sug­gests, travel like tim­ber: ab­stract re­searchers pro­duce them, ap­plied re­searchers turn them into pol­icy ideas, and jour­nal­ists and in­tel­lec­tu­als carry them to the pub­lic. {062-C01}
Ajay Shah said the land­scape has changed. He de­scribed a “physics il­lu­sion” in the so­cial sci­ences, the hope of sin­gle grand the­o­ries that apply ev­ery­where.

Instead, eco­nom­ics has be­come a set of sub­cul­tures, each work­ing on one dataset. The 20 peo­ple who know the CMIE house­hold sur­vey, he said, share code and con­cepts, read each other’s pa­pers and cite each other. {#cmie}
“It’s bet­ter to be loyal to the re­al­ity rather than set­tle for a sweet ab­strac­tion,” Shah said. {062-C02}
## A paper, not a pub

For the episode, Shah set aside the jour­nal ar­ti­cle as the mean­ing of “paper”. A paper is any build­ing block of new knowl­edge, and knowl­edge is a graph of such pa­pers, used by in­di­vid­u­als, firms and gov­ern­ments.
Journals, he said, now serve only as cre­den­tials. A ma­ture reader can judge a paper di­rectly: does it give me a new idea, does it make me change my mind? {062-C04}

~ Knowing the so­ci­ol­ogy of how this ma­chine works, Shah said, helps a reader “shrug off some of the show­boat­ing” that au­thors do to get pub­lished. {062-J13} Varma de­clared it the phrase that em­bod­ies the show.

quote.text: Today the dis­sem­i­na­tion func­tion is 100% gone. You never need to go to the jour­nal web­site to get the paper.

sections.label: The three tests
sections.head: Is it new? Is it true?
sections.caption: the three tests of a paper
body: Every paper in sci­ence or so­cial sci­ence, Ajay Shah said, needs three things: clar­ity on a ques­tion, an an­swer that per­suades rather than mak­ing “some ran­dom claims”, and nov­elty. {062-C05}
A sum­mary of the state of the art is use­ful, he said, but it is not a paper. “You could ex­pect a LLM to read 20 pa­pers and sum­marise them.” {#llm}
The same tests make a good ref­eree re­port. Shah would ask a re­viewer to write down the paper’s ques­tion and its an­swer afresh. In a con­fused paper, nei­ther can be read­ily culled out.
## Whose ques­tion mat­ters?

Then there is im­por­tance. Global warm­ing is prob­a­bly im­por­tant, Shah said, and the head­gear of some trib­als in Chandrapur dis­trict prob­a­bly is not. But “im­por­tance is in the eye of the be­holder”. {062-C06}

Amit Varma raised “the rad­i­cal pos­si­bil­ity that the head­gear of the Chandrapur trib­als causes global warm­ing”. Shah, straight-faced, won­dered about ob­scure chem­i­cals in the head­gear trig­ger­ing re­ac­tions in the upper at­mos­phere. {062-J03}

~ Researchers do not waste their time, Shah ar­gued. If some­one has put real ef­fort into a ques­tion, oth­ers should as­sume it mat­ters to some­one, as the es­tab­lish­ment failed to see with every mav­er­ick. {#time}

quote.text: What’s the ques­tion? Is the clar­ity on the ques­tion? What’s the an­swer? Is the an­swer per­sua­sive? And a test. Is it novel?

sections.label: The reader first
sections.head: It takes two to write
sections.caption: putting the reader first
body: Amit Varma put to Ajay Shah the ques­tion he asks in the first we­bi­nar of his writ­ing course. We learn many dif­fi­cult things eas­ily, so why do we fail at com­mu­ni­cat­ing, even with friends in a cafe or with a loved one?
Shah’s an­swer pointed to Broca’s area, the part of the brain that does speech. Varma called it “a deeply tech­ni­cal an­swer” that was “ab­so­lutely cor­rect”. {062-J06}

His own an­swer: learn­ing has one vari­able, your­self, while com­mu­ni­cat­ing has two. Writing, he said, only be­comes mean­ing­ful when it has the in­tended ef­fect on the in­tended reader. {062-C08}
## The life story can wait
Shah agreed, and turned on his own pro­fes­sion. Researchers cut cor­ners on writ­ing, he said, and that is wrong: the pur­pose of a paper is to change the mind of a cyn­i­cal reader. {062-C09}
Research is a moun­tain climb of fum­bles, dead ends and aha mo­ments, but the paper should leave the climb out. “They don’t want to know your life story,” Shah said of read­ers. {062-C10}
~ The jour­ney can also change the des­ti­na­tion, he added: set out for India and you may find the route to America. {#india} Then you write about the route to America.

quote.text: Communicating is tough be­cause there are two vari­ables.

sections.label: The skeleton
sections.head: Structure before swagger
sections.caption: the structure of a paper
body: Beginners, Ajay Shah said, should stick to stan­dard struc­tures. Once they find their pow­ers, they can smash the bound­aries. {062-C11}

In sci­ence, the de­fault is IMRD. {#imrd} The in­tro­duc­tion sum­marises what is known and ends with the ques­tions. Methods must be de­tailed enough for third par­ties to repli­cate the work. Results re­port what was found with­out much in­ter­pre­ta­tion; dis­cus­sion asks what it means and where re­search should go next.

Shah called it “a low bull­shit way to do sci­en­tific com­mu­ni­ca­tion”. He had also cited the Leap Blog with­out ex­plain­ing it, and Amit Varma caught him: “You just com­mit­ted the curse of knowl­edge.” {062-J07}
## The economist’s recipe

For eco­nom­ics, Shah uses a title, a 100-word ab­stract, and an in­tro­duc­tion that is re­ally a 1,000-word ex­ec­u­tive sum­mary, often pub­lished sep­a­rately in a news­pa­per or on a blog. Then come the set­ting and ques­tions, meth­ods and re­sults, ro­bust­ness checks against al­ter­na­tive ex­pla­na­tions, and a con­clu­sion that asks: so what?
Most care goes to the top. “A hun­dred thou­sand peo­ple are going to read the title of your paper, so make it count,” Shah said. {062-C12}
~ Brevity is work too. Varma quoted Blaise Pascal, who ended a long let­ter to a friend: “I’m sorry this let­ter is so long, I did not have time to make it short.” {062-J18}

quote.text: as you grow up, you find your pow­ers, then you can smash the bound­aries and do things in novel ways

sections.label: The act of writing
sections.head: Inside out, title last
sections.caption: writing inside out
body: Writing changes your mind as you go, Ajay Shah said, so the tidy plan of title first, then ab­stract, then paper rarely works. Amit Varma reached for Joan Didion: “I write to find out what I think.” {062-J19}
Shah writes in­side out: the body of the paper first, then the con­clu­sions. “Then write the in­tro­duc­tion. Then write the ab­stract and last write the title.” {#insideout}

Writing is costly, he said, but don’t love text just be­cause you pro­duced it. When a chunk is weak he deletes it and starts again, “be­cause I find the mind is cleaner when writ­ing from scratch”. {062-C13}
## A slideshow no­body sees
His teams build each paper first as an in­ter­nal slideshow of 40 to 50 slides, with every table, graph and ci­ta­tion in the order of the ar­gu­ment. Every meet­ing turns up er­rors and new ideas.

The as­sis­tants, who are ap­pren­tices, im­ple­ment them. Each time, Shah said, they must come back “with an ab­so­lutely per­fect prod­uct in the opin­ion of the ap­pren­tice”. {#apprentice} When the meet­ings stop pro­duc­ing changes, the search has con­verged, and the slides be­come prose.

~ Varma set this apart from Jeff Bezos’s rule at Amazon, “do not bring me an eff­ing pow­er­point”: a pre­sen­ta­tion sim­pli­fies, while this deck holds ev­ery­thing. Shah agreed that it is only an in­ter­nal tech­nique to reach the paper. {062-C14}

quote.text: So we should never take this slideshow and try to take it to an au­di­ence. This is just a de­vel­op­ment plat­form.

sections.label: Lessons learnt
sections.head: The long apprenticeship
sections.caption: a lifetime of learning the craft
body: Asked what years of writ­ing pa­pers had taught him, Ajay Shah began with a con­fes­sion: when he was young, he grossly un­der­es­ti­mated how hard it would be. {062-S07}
He read pa­pers early and as­sumed he would slide from read­ing them to writ­ing them. He was wrong. Writing pa­pers, he said, is a craft, and like every craft it takes prac­tice.

He has learnt in two ways. He looks back dis­pas­sion­ately at what he did a year or two ago, and he stud­ies pa­pers that leave him “shocked at how per­fect and how well done this is”, ask­ing how the au­thors did it. {#shocked}
## Life after the PhD

A PhD does not fin­ish the train­ing, Shah said. Fresh PhDs often feel ready to go and write pa­pers; un­for­tu­nately, he said, that is not true. It takes many years after the PhD to imag­ine a re­search project and get it done in a lead­er­ship role. {062-C16}
“It’s a very long child­hood, it’s a long ap­pren­tice­ship where peo­ple learn,” he said. {#childhood}
~ His ad­vice to ev­ery­one was to ap­proach the work “with a suit­able level of re­spect that you’re going to climb a moun­tain”. {#mountain}

quote.text: When I was young, I was a lit­tle too op­ti­mistic that it will be easy, I’ll tran­si­tion from read­ing pa­pers to writ­ing pa­pers.
Think of the reader. I wish to say some­thing to the reader. I wish to change the mind of the reader, which is very hard.

p3.title: Tales from the paper trail
p3.deck: Four stories from Ajay Shah’s decades of writing papers, and what they teach

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a title that kept luring him back
stories.head: The title that cried wolf
body: There is one paper Ajay Shah will not name, and he will not name its au­thors ei­ther. But its title, he said, is very cute, and he has thought about it for years.
The title dragged him back to read the paper sev­eral times. Each time, the paper was not about the title. {062-S04}

“Titles should not just be cute, they should also be about the paper,” Shah said. A title is a one-sentence sum­mary, and a lit­er­ary flour­ish helps. But the urge for cute­ness, he thinks, is a bit over­done.

Amit Varma of­fered one that gets it right. In the early 1990s, as Varma re­called, Vijayendra Rao stud­ied dowry and how it was chang­ing, and called his paper *The Rising Price of Husbands*. “It’s clever and it is about the paper,” Varma said. {062-R07}

Shah of­fered one of his own, writ­ten with col­leagues in­clud­ing Ayush Patnaik and Susan Thomas: *But Clouds Got in My Way*. “What a great title,” said Varma. It is about clouds, Shah ex­plained: clouds in­ter­fer­ing with in­frared ra­di­a­tion going up to a satel­lite.
Varma later pic­tured the end of that la­bo­ri­ous paper: the au­thors sit­ting back, putting on some Joni Mitchell, and find­ing the line in “the great song”, *Both Sides Now*. {062-R09}
~ The stakes are high, Shah said, be­cause the title is what most read­ers will ever see. Of 100,000 who see it, about 100 will fin­ish the paper.
stories.why: A title is the one sen­tence most read­ers will ever see. Wit can earn their at­ten­tion, but a title that is not about the paper wastes it, and the author’s cred­i­bil­ity too. The best, like Rao’s, are clever and ac­cu­rate at once.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on cute titles and good ones

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how journals began, and what they are for now
stories.head: From letters to letterheads
body: Research com­mu­ni­ca­tion, Ajay Shah said, began with a let­ter. A sci­en­tist would write to the Secretary of the Royal Society in London to say: I did this new work. {062-S01}
The Secretary gath­ered these let­ters into a pub­li­ca­tion that went out to all the mem­bers. Out of those be­gin­nings grew mod­ern jour­nals, and their job was dis­sem­i­na­tion.

That job, Shah said, is now “100% gone”. Mature work­ing pa­pers, blog ar­ti­cles and news­pa­per ar­ti­cles carry im­por­tant new knowl­edge, and no­body needs a jour­nal web­site to get a paper. Journals sur­vive as brand names that help you get a job or a grant. {062-C04}
~ The world, he said, is back to the Royal Society’s un­struc­tured, ev­ery­one-to-everyone model. Amit Varma noted one dif­fer­ence: today there is no Royal Society in be­tween.
stories.why: Institutions can out­live their pur­pose and be­come cre­den­tial ma­chines. Once you see that jour­nals cer­tify ca­reers rather than spread knowl­edge, Shah ar­gued, you can judge a paper on its mer­its, not on where it ap­peared.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Royal Society’s letters

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the work that starts when writing ends
stories.head: The flood after the press
body: In *The Outlaws*, an ear­lier episode, Ajay Shah re­called, he had shared a piece of trivia: Mendel or­dered forty copies of his paper from the press. {062-S03}
Today there is no such limit. “At the same time, the world is del­uged with too much rub­bish,” Shah said. Put a fin­ished paper on a web­site and the world is not wait­ing to read it.

So the work con­tin­ues after the writ­ing: news­pa­per pieces, blog posts, a video, talks. Small rooms mat­ter, he said, be­cause when you are put into a room with two hun­dred peo­ple and given ten min­utes, noth­ing gets done. {#room200}

~ Skip it, he warned, and a hun­dred years from now fa­mous YouTubers will make a show about your paper on the web­site of IIM Kozhikode, “but no­body in this world both­ered to read that paper”. {062-J10}

quote.text: it’s a stone that will just skip over the lake and it’ll be gone

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Mendel’s forty copies

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the order of names on a paper
stories.head: S before T, nothing more
body: Amit Varma pointed out that Ajay Shah’s most fre­quent co-author is Susan Thomas. When peo­ple see a Shah and Thomas paper, Shah said, they as­sume it is be­cause he is “the cool guy”. {062-S05}
In fact the names are al­pha­bet­i­cal. Her work or role, he said, is in no way in­fe­rior to his: S sim­ply comes be­fore T.

Shah likes the con­ven­tion be­cause it leaves only one fight, over whether you get au­thor­ship at all. Once you do, ev­ery­one is equal. Otherwise, he said, the pos­si­ble or­der­ings mul­ti­ply to n-factorial, and there is fight upon fight.

~ Varma, whose sur­name starts with V, re­called re­search from Malcolm Gladwell’s *Outliers*: top ath­letes tend to be born early in the year, be­cause age-group cut-offs fall on 1 January. {#january} He was born in December. “I had no chance.” {062-J12}
stories.why: A good con­ven­tion re­moves a fight that would oth­er­wise hap­pen. It also means read­ers should not read hi­er­ar­chy into au­thor order with­out know­ing the rules of the field. Different com­mu­ni­ties, Shah said, play by dif­fer­ent rules.

quiz.q: What three things, according to Ajay Shah, does every paper in science or social science need?
quiz.a: A clearly stated ques­tion, a per­sua­sive an­swer, and nov­elty in the work.

quiz.q: What do the letters IMRD stand for in the standard structure of a science paper?
quiz.a: Introduction, meth­ods, re­sults and dis­cus­sion: the de­fault skele­ton of a STEM paper.

quiz.q: Why does Shah often delete a weak chunk of a paper rather than edit it?
quiz.a: He finds the mind is cleaner writ­ing from scratch than tin­ker­ing with old stuff.

quiz.q: Which song did Amit Varma imagine giving *But Clouds Got in My Way* its title?
quiz.a: Joni Mitchell’s *Both Sides Now*, which Varma called “the great song”.

quiz.q: Why does Shah prefer a room of ten people to a room of two hundred?
quiz.a: Thirty to fifty min­utes with ten fo­cused peo­ple ac­tu­ally changes minds.

quiz.q: What, according to Amit Varma, makes communicating harder than learning difficult things?
quiz.a: Learning in­volves one vari­able, your­self; com­mu­ni­cat­ing in­volves two, you and the other per­son.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 62. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Joan Didion (Kathleen Ballard, Los Angeles Times, CC BY 4.0); Joni Mitchell (Library of Congress Life, CC0); Deirdre McCloskey (Policy Exchange, CC BY 2.0).

shelf.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s his­tory of the big eco­nomic de­bates of the last cen­tury, from Keynes and Friedman to Fabian so­cial­ism and cen­tral plan­ning, show­ing that each school was right in some ways and wrong in oth­ers.

shelf.title: Larry White episode of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s mas­ter­class on free bank­ing: banks is­su­ing their own com­pet­ing cur­ren­cies ran for decades in parts of the world with­out chaos.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: The Outlaws (Episode 61)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Stories of mav­er­icks such as Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin who were ig­nored by the es­tab­lish­ment and vin­di­cated late, some­times at the cost of lives.

shelf.title: CMIE Household Survey
shelf.creator: CMIE
shelf.why: CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey (about 190,000 house­holds, three times a year, across some 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions) makes India’s di­ver­sity mea­sur­able, from five­fold in­come gaps be­tween re­gions to how many house­holds re­ally live off farm­ing.

shelf.title: The Leap Blog
shelf.why: The peer-reviewed re­search blog Ajay co-edits, where his ideas are avail­able to any­one at any time.

shelf.title: The Rising Price of Husbands
shelf.creator: Vijayendra Rao
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite ti­tles: clever and also ac­cu­rately about the paper.

shelf.title: But Clouds Got In My Way: Bias And Bias Correction Of VIIRS Nighttime Lights Data In The Presence Of Clouds
shelf.creator: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal and Susan Thomas
shelf.why: Ajay’s group’s paper doc­u­ment­ing a cloud-related bias in NASA/NOAA night­time-lights data, with a con­ser­va­tive cor­rec­tion; the data mea­sures pros­per­ity monthly at half-kilometre res­o­lu­tion with­out de­pend­ing on the gov­ern­ment.

shelf.title: Both Sides Now
shelf.creator: Joni Mitchell
shelf.why: ‘The great song’, as Amit calls it, which gave Ajay’s paper But Clouds Got In My Way its title.

shelf.title: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
shelf.creator: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
shelf.why: A clear, rig­or­ous paper ar­gu­ing that the state should ‘buy’ rather than ‘make’ in­no­va­tion by con­tract­ing R&D out, with a con­crete 20-year blue­print.

shelf.title: Outliers
shelf.creator: Malcolm Gladwell
shelf.why: Where Amit learned the re­search on elite ath­letes being born early in the year, a vivid case of a triv­ial-looking dis­tri­bu­tion with real ef­fects.

shelf.title: The Elements of Style
shelf.creator: William Strunk Jr and EB White
shelf.why: The clas­sic state­ment of clar­ity and brevity, val­ues Bell Labs car­ried into pro­gram­ming; Ajay says ‘the sim­ple Strunk and White’ should be uni­ver­sal knowl­edge for ev­ery­one doing re­search.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Economical Writing
shelf.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
shelf.why: McCloskey shows how to write about eco­nom­ics, or any com­plex sub­ject, so that lay read­ers find it clear and in­ter­est­ing: ex­actly what Amit’s stu­dents from jar­gon-rewarding fields like so­ci­ol­ogy and an­thro­pol­ogy need.

shelf.title: Does the currency regime shape unhedged currency exposure
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of Ajay’s cho­sen favourite pa­pers in­volv­ing him­self.

shelf.title: Trade misinvoicing: A channel for de facto capital account openness
shelf.creator: Abhijit Sen Gupta, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of Ajay’s cho­sen favourite pa­pers in­volv­ing him­self.

shelf.title: Are fleeting orders by high frequency traders a source of market abuse?
shelf.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal and Chirag Anand
shelf.why: One of Ajay’s cho­sen favourites; it ap­peared on the Leap Blog.

shelf.title: The Lowest Hanging Fruit On The Coconut Tree: India’s Climate Transition Through The Price System In The Power Sector
shelf.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay’s case for a mar­ket-based elec­tric­ity sec­tor that drives India’s cli­mate tran­si­tion through the price sys­tem, rather than the state pick­ing favoured tech­nolo­gies.

laughs.text: Ajay on re­search guid­ing in­di­vid­ual choices: to de­cide whether to go to col­lege, ‘first you should get a PhD and learn to read the pa­pers about the gains from col­lege... Because if you haven’t read those pa­pers, how can you make a de­ci­sion about whether or not it’s worth going to col­lege?’ Amit: ‘This is a trap.’

Amit, on Ajay’s Chandrapur ex­am­ple: ‘There is also the rad­i­cal pos­si­bil­ity that the head­gear of the Chandrapur trib­als causes global warm­ing.’ Ajay plays along with a straight face, sug­gest­ing ob­scure chem­i­cals in the head­gear could trig­ger re­ac­tions in the upper at­mos­phere. Amit: ‘I didn’t ex­pect you to riff off my im­ma­ture quip, but con­tinue.’

Amit, after Ajay says jour­nals only re­ward small in­cre­men­tal moves: ‘You and I should throw a party where we call every aca­demic we know and we get them com­pletely drunk, and then we gather a bunch of jour­nals and we have a bon­fire of the jour­nals.’
Asked why we fail to com­mu­ni­cate, Ajay brings up Broca’s area, the part of the brain that han­dles speech. Amit: ‘That’s a deeply tech­ni­cal an­swer and it is ab­so­lutely cor­rect.’
Ajay men­tions the Leap Blog with­out ex­plain­ing it, and Amit catches him: ‘You just com­mit­ted the curse of knowl­edge.’

Ajay on skip­ping self-promotion: a hun­dred years from now, fa­mous YouTubers will make a show about the amaz­ing paper you posted on the web­site of IIM Kozhikode, ‘but no­body in this world both­ered to read that paper.’

Amit’s the­ory of al­pha­bet­i­cal in­jus­tice: would he have writ­ten more pa­pers if his name were Ahluwalia? Hayek, Friedman, Keynes and Arrow all sit early in the al­pha­bet. ‘There’s no great econ­o­mist called Zimbalist.’ Ajay turns it into a re­search project: test whether the first let­ters of econ Nobel laureates’ sur­names dif­fer sig­nif­i­cantly from the gen­eral pop­u­la­tion.

Karl Marx’s epi­taph, cited by Ajay to dis­tin­guish re­search that only seeks to un­der­stand the world from re­search meant to act on it: the philoso­phers have tried to un­der­stand the world; ‘the point, how­ever, is to change it.’
Blaise Pascal, quoted by Amit: ‘I’m sorry this let­ter is so long, I did not have time to make it short.’
Joan Didion, quoted by Amit: ‘I write to find out what I think.’ He uses it to sup­port Ajay’s point that writ­ing changes the ar­gu­ment as you go.
Paul Graham’s line, which Amit has adopted: ‘It’s bet­ter to be loved by a few than liked by many.’
